stress.notes: Standard Spanish accentuation (inherited from es-ES): default paroxytone; written accent wins; oxytone before consonant codas other than n/s; proparoxytones always written-accented. Final -y after a vowel: the letter writes the off-glide of a falling diphthong, 'en los diptongos ai, ei, oi, que a veces se escriben en la forma ay, ey, oy, la i (y) se pronuncia ... más corta' (ley [ˈlei̯], buey, soy; Navarro Tomás 1918, Manual de pronunciación española, § 47, p. 39), and § 50, p. 41 repeats that the written y of ley, rey, doy, soy 'se pronuncia como i'. For accentuation such a word counts as consonant-final: oxytones ending in -y take no tilde (guirigay, virrey, convoy, estoy) and paroxytones ending in -y do (yérsey, yóquey) (RAE-ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas, 2nd ed., s.v. tilde, § 1.2.1-1.2.2). The endings ay, ey, oy, uy encode that rule. A consonant+y ending is not a Spanish spelling: rugby and sexy are unadapted English forms whose adaptations are rugbi and sexi (DPD s.v. rugbi, sexi), so they keep the default paroxytone.
